summary: Lisboa is a dense, puzzly Lacerda design where every action ripples across half a dozen interlocking systems — building tiles, ships, wigs, factories, and disaster markers all pull on the same few resources. Turns are quiet and heads-down as players optimize multi-use cards and timing rather than clash directly, with the game rewarding a long-term engine plan over reactive play.
praised: Tight, elegant interlocking of systems for how much is going on
Multi-use cards create constant meaningful trade-offs
Thematic tie to the Lisbon earthquake reconstruction is well integrated into mechanisms
High replayability from variable card draws and multiple viable strategies
criticised: Steep learning curve and dense rulebook/iconography
Low direct interaction can make it feel like solitaire at the same table
Production/component overhead (small tiles, many trackers) can feel fiddly

interaction.kind: mostly parallel play with some indirect competition over tile placement and card availability

scoring.why: Points accumulate from building placement, factories, ships, wigs, and end-game bonuses, so the winner is whoever best converts an efficient engine into the most scoring avenues
